aflcio_description: The inability of the Senate to override President Ford's veto of a third major jobs bill passed by the 94th Congress doomed thousands of American workers to continued unemployment. The public works employment bill would have created over 600,000 jobs in construction of badly needed public projects such as schools and libraries and sewer and water treatment facilities. The legislation also contained $1.5 billion in aid to financially-strapped cities and states primarily to prevent cutbacks in services and potential lay-offs of an estimated 100,000 local government workers. The Senate vote of 63-35 on Feb. 19 in favor of overriding the veto was three votes short of the two-thirds voted needed for override. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

A second, scaled-down version of the public works jobs bill also felt the sting of President Ford's veto. This time, however, Congress overwhelmingly overrode that action. The second bill, a $3.9 billion package would create over 300,000 jobs, maintained over $1 billion in aid to cities. On July 21 the Senate easily overrode this veto by a 73-24 vote. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

President Ford vetoed the 1976 Labor-HEW appropriations bill, charging that the increased federal funding for such programs as health research, vocational rehabilitation, alcohol and drug abuse prevention, and community service programs was "wasteful." The Senate followed the House's lead and rejected Ford's veto in a lopsided 70-24 vote on Jan. 28. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

A stopgap funding bill to help state child care centers comply with federal health and staffing requirements was vetoed by President Ford raising the prospect that financially hard-pressed states would have to close down many of these facilities. And without the availability of such child care services, many low-income working mothers would be forced onto welfare. The Senate on May 5 failed to override the veto by a 60-34 vote, three votes short of the needed two-thirds. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

A 1977 housing authorization bill which increased housing funds for the elderly and resurrected public housing funding was strongly opposed by the Ford Administration. Successive Republican Administrations had refused to spend funds allocated by Congress for public housing construction. Conservatives led by Sen. Garn (R-Utah) made a last minute effort to recommit the conference report on the housing bill to have these provisions eliminated. The Senate rejected Garn's recommittal motion by a 23-57 vote on Apr. 27. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Under the current tax laws, U.S.-based multinational corporations pay no U.S. taxes on profits earned overseas unless the money is returned to the United States, which could be never. This tax subsidy effectively encourages these firms to shift major segments of their industries overseas. It is estimated that since 1966 this loophole has cost the nation over 1 million jobs. During debate on a major tax bill Sen. Hartke (D-Ind.) sponsored a labor-backed amendment to tax the profits at the U.S. tax rate at the time they are earned. His amendment would have phased out this tax escape over a five-year period. However, the Senate voted to kill the measure, first tabling it and then by a 45-44 vote on June 29 tabled the motion to reconsider. For Tabling - Wrong. Against Tabling - Right.

A second try to close this foreign profits loophole met with a similar fate. Sen. Hollings (D-S.C.), pointing to the increased revenues to be gained both by taxing multinational firms and by preserving domestic employment, offered a similar version of the previously defeated Hartke provision. The Senate again rejected the proposal 31-43 on Aug. 6. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The Senate committee's tax bill significantly weakened House-passed provisions limiting tax shelters used by wealthy doctors, lawyers and executives. During debate on the bill, labor supported an amendment by Sen. Nelson (D-Wis.) to restore the House provision limiting opportunities for wealthy Americans to use paper losses in non-residential real estate, gas and oil leasing, movies, farms and sports franchises to avoid taxes. The Senate, however, on June 17 agreed 46-33 to a motion by Sen. Long (D-La.) to table and thus kill the Nelson amendment. For Tabling - Wrong. Against Tabling - Right.

On June 24 the Senate rejected a labor-backed proposal by Sen. Mondale (D-Minn.) to tighten the minimum tax provision so as to extract a minimum amount of tax from wealthy individuals who use various gimmicks to avoid normal taxation. His amendment would have raised the minimum tax rate from 10 to 15 percent, cut the exemption to $10,000 in preference income and eliminated the present deduction for taxes paid. The Senate tabled this amendment, 45-39, on a motion by Sen. Long (D-La.) which killed the reform. For Tabling - Wrong. Against Tabling - Right.

As debate progressed on the Senate version of the tax bill the legislation became so riddled with new tax loopholes that the end result could cost the federal government over $300 million in fiscal 1977 and billions more in later years. After opening up new loopholes for corporations and wealthy individuals, the Senate tried to recoup some of these lost revenues by wiping out the tax exclusion allowed on a portion of pay received by workers during illnesses, one of the few genuine tax breaks for those in need. An amendment by Sen. Bayh (D-Ind.), approved 48-34 on Aug. 6, retained the sick pay exclusion for those earning $15,000 or less yearly. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

During Senate debate on legislation reconstructing the Federal Election Commission (FEC), anti-labor forces sought to simply resurrect the commission and thereby kill a number of campaign finance reforms approved by the Senate Rules Committee. As reported by the committee the bill amended existing campaign financing laws to prohibit anti-labor regulations previously approved by the FEC. Sen. Griffin (R-Mich.) introduced a substitute bill to resurrect the commission and leave its anti-labor regulations intact. The Griffin bill was rejected 39-55 on Mar. 18. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

The 1939 Political Activity Act, commonly known as the Hatch Act, now prohibits some 2.8 million federal and postal employees from participating in partisan political activities. Reform legislation designed to correct this inequity while also strengthening existing restrictions against political coercion of federal workers passed the House in 1975. Although the bill was later vetoed, the Senate passed its version of Hatch Act reform on Mar. 11 by a 47-32 vote. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The Senate Agriculture Committee reported regressive legislation that would have eliminated millions of needy families from the food stamp program. To prevent passage of this legislation, the AFL-CIO endorsed a compromise substitute bill by Senators McGovern (D-S.D.) and Dole (R-Kans.) which, while tightening up requirements, maintained the eligibility status of those truly in need. The Senate approved the compromise measure, 49-30, on Apr. 8. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

One of the major problems in dealing with the nation's energy crisis is congressional inability to obtain, either directly or through federal agencies, accurate information on energy supplies, costs, and needs. To correct this situation, Sen. Haskell (D-Colo.) during Senate debate on an extension of the Federal Energy Act, offered an amendment to create within the Federal Energy Administration an independent office to gather, analyze, and provide Congress with information on the nation's supply and consumption of energy. The new agency was authorized to collect financial data from energy companies as well as other information regarding separate energy activities of the industry. Despite strong industry opposition, the Senate approved Haskell's amendment by a narrow 46-45 vote on June 15. It was later modified in conference. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

aflcio_description: Under pressure from the Ford Administration, trial lawyers and some insurance companies, the Senate voted to scuttle a labor-backed no-fault auto insurance bill. This important consumer reform legislation was designed to assure auto accident victims adequate and more timely compensation of losses, better allocation of their premium dollars and lower insurance costs. The legislation was pigeonholed, however, as the Senate by a 45-47 vote on Mar. 31, refused to reconsider its vote to recommit the bill and thus killed it. For Reconsideration - Right. Against Reconsideration - Wrong.

Recognizing the inadequacies in the federal enforcement of antitrust laws against monopolistic practices, the AFL-CIO has urged corrective legislative action to protect the consumer and marketplace competition. In 1976 labor supported antitrust reform legislation which, among other provisions, would allow state attorneys general to bring antitrust suits on behalf of citizens. Despite earlier support, the Ford Administration switched signals under pressure from big business and opposed the measure. As a result, Senate conservatives filibustered the legislation in hopes of killing it. However, on June 3 the Senate by a 67-22 vote invoked cloture and thereby cut off debate. The Senate later passed the legislation. For Cloture - Right. Against Cloture - Wrong.

During Senate debate on a supplemental appropriations bill, Sen. Kennedy (D-Mass.) tried to increase by $1 billion the funding for elementary and secondary education assistance to disadvantaged children. At present, because of the lack of funds, only about 50 percent of the children eligible for this educational aid are served by the program. The Senate, however, rejected Kennedy's amendment, 25-64, on May 11. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

During Senate debate on a 1977 military construction authorization bill, anti-labor forces renewed their attack on the prevailing wage provisions of the Davis-Bacon Act. An amendment by Sen. Tower (R-Tex.) would have prohibited the payment of Davis-Bacon prevailing wage rates to construction workers at military projects. The Senate easily rejected this amendment 17-66 on May 20. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Opponents of the B-1 bomber renewed their attacks on continued development of this weapons system in the second session. Although unsuccessful in their efforts to block this program in 1975, the Senate reversed its direction, approving a proposal by Sen. Culver (D-Iowa) to the 1977 Defense Procurement Authorization bill disallowing the expenditure of funds for B-1 until after Feb. 1, 1977. By a 44-37 vote on May 20 the Senate accepted Culver's amendment. The amendment was later eliminated in conference. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

The AFL-CIO has long supported federal incentives to encourage efficient solid waste recycling programs. At the same time, the federation has opposed efforts to impose any kind of so-called ban-the-can legislation because of its severe impact on domestic employment and increased cost to consumers. During Senate debate on legislation providing federal funds for state and local solid waste programs through 1979, Sen. Hatfield (R-Ore.) offered a "ban-the-can" amendment. His proposal would have imposed a mandatory 5-cent deposit on all beer and soft drink cans and bottles within five years while banning "pop-top" beverage cans within one year. Strongly opposed by labor, his amendment was rejected 26-60 on June 30. For - Wrong. Against - Right.
